rashtrakuta-empire.name: Rashtrakuta Empire
rashtrakuta-empire.summary: Early medieval Indian empire (6th–10th centuries) ruling from the Ganges to the south, noted for architecture, literature, and elevating Kannada alongside Sanskrit.

ellora-caves.name: Ellora
ellora-caves.summary: A UNESCO World Heritage rock-cut cave complex in India with over 100 Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves carved from basalt cliffs between about 600 and 1000 CE.

nagara-style.name: Nagara style
nagara-style.summary: A Hindu temple architecture style found across northern, central, western and eastern India, marked by curved spires and no boundary walls; one of the two main Hindu temple styles.

dravidian-architecture.name: Dravidian architecture
dravidian-architecture.summary: A South Indian temple-building style reaching its final form by the 16th century, marked by shorter, pyramidal towers over the sanctuary and, in larger temples, tall gateway towers.

pattadakal.name: Pattadakal
pattadakal.summary: A UNESCO World Heritage complex of 7th- and 8th-century Hindu and Jain temples in Karnataka, India, blending northern and southern Indian architectural styles.

aihole.name: Aihole
aihole.summary: A historic site in Karnataka, India, with over 120 Hindu, Jain and Buddhist stone temples dating from the 6th to 12th centuries CE.

chaitya.name: Chaitya hall
chaitya.summary: A shrine or prayer hall in Indian religions, most often a Buddhist space with a stupa, a rounded apse and a high curved roof, frequently carved directly into rock.

sirpur-mahasamund.name: Sirpur
sirpur-mahasamund.summary: A village in Chhattisgarh, India, that was capital of the Panduvanshi dynasty and hosts a group of Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monuments from the 5th to 12th centuries.

rajim.name: Rajim
rajim.summary: A Hindu pilgrimage town in Chhattisgarh, India, named for its temple to Vishnu and called the 'Prayag of Chhattisgarh' for its river confluence.

vastu-shastra.name: Vastu Shastra
vastu-shastra.summary: A traditional Hindu system of architecture from ancient India describing design, layout and spatial principles meant to align buildings with nature, sunlight, wind and other natural forces.

muhammad-ibn-al-qasim.name: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim
muhammad-ibn-al-qasim.summary: Arab military commander who led the Umayyad conquest of Sindh from 708 to 711, becoming the first Muslim to capture Indian territory, and died in 715.

dahir-of-aror.name: Raja Dahir
dahir-of-aror.summary: Last maharaja of Sindh (695–712), a Brahmin ruler killed in 712 when the Umayyad Caliphate under Muhammad ibn al-Qasim invaded his kingdom.

battle-of-aror.name: Battle of Aror
battle-of-aror.summary: A 712 AD battle in which Umayyad forces under Muhammad ibn al-Qasim defeated Raja Dahir of Sindh's Brahmin dynasty near the Indus River, the last battle Dahir fought before his death.

sindh.name: Sindh
sindh.summary: A province of Pakistan along the Indus River, home to early South Asian settlement and later conquered by Arab forces in 712 CE.

sabuktigin.name: Sabuktigin
sabuktigin.summary: Founder of the Ghaznavid dynasty who ruled as amir of Ghazna from 977 to 997, a former Turkic slave soldier who expanded his rule into Afghanistan and India.

jayapala.name: Jayapala
jayapala.summary: A ruler of the Hindu Shahi dynasty from 964 to 1001, controlling territory from Lamghan to Kashmir and Sirhind to Multan, whose realm came under pressure from Ghaznavid expansion.

hindu-shahis.name: Hindu Shahis
hindu-shahis.summary: A dynasty that ruled Kabulistan, Gandhara and Punjab from 822 to 1026 CE, eventually falling to the Ghaznavids after decades of resistance.

laghman-province.name: Laghman
laghman-province.summary: A province in eastern Afghanistan, historically known as Lamghan, noted for its many historical landmarks and monuments.

ghaznavid-empire.name: Ghaznavid Empire
ghaznavid-empire.summary: Persianate Muslim empire of Turkic origin that flourished from 977 to 1186, stretching at its height from the Oxus River to the Indus Valley.

chalukya-dynasty.name: Chalukya dynasty
chalukya-dynasty.summary: An Indian dynasty, split into three related branches, that ruled large parts of southern and central India from the 6th to the 12th centuries and is seen as a golden age in Karnataka's history.

pallava-dynasty.name: Pallava dynasty
pallava-dynasty.summary: A dynasty ruling parts of southern India from 275 to 897 CE, reaching its height under Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I and known for patronizing Hindu temple architecture and the Pallava script.

kanchipuram.name: Kanchipuram
kanchipuram.summary: A city in Tamil Nadu, India, known as the 'City of Thousand Temples' for its temple architecture and historically ruled by the Pallavas and other dynasties.

pandya-dynasty.name: Pandya dynasty
pandya-dynasty.summary: An ancient Tamil dynasty of South India, one of the three great Tamil kingdoms, ruling with varying extent from about 400 BCE to 1618 CE.

debal.name: Debal
debal.summary: An ancient port and commercial town in Sindh, in present-day Pakistan, whose exact location remains uncertain and which was mainly inhabited by the Med tribe.

chach-nama.name: Chach Nama
chach-nama.summary: A historical text on the conquest of Sindh, presented as a 13th-century account of the early 8th-century Arab conquest, whose authenticity and reliability are disputed by modern historians.

k-s-lal.name: K. S. Lal
k-s-lal.summary: Indian Hindu nationalist historian (1920–2002) who wrote several works on the medieval history of India.

abu-ali-lawik.name: Abu Ali Lawik
abu-ali-lawik.summary: Son of Abu Bakr Lawik of the Lawik dynasty and brother-in-law of the Hindu Shahi ruler; he was invited by the people of Ghazni to overthrow its cruel ruler and marched with Shahi allies to retake it, but was defeated by Sabuktigin at Charkh.

ghazni.name: Ghazni
ghazni.summary: City in southeastern Afghanistan, historically the capital of the Ghaznavid Empire and today the capital of Ghazni Province.

charkh-district.name: Charkh
charkh-district.summary: A district and village in Logar Province, Afghanistan, home to the tomb of the scholar Mawlana Yaqoub Charkhi.

vizhinjam.name: Vizhinjam
vizhinjam.summary: Coastal area in the city of Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala, India, now home to India's first deep-water transshipment port.

ay-dynasty.name: Ay dynasty
ay-dynasty.summary: An Indian dynasty that ruled the southwestern tip of the Kerala peninsula, controlling the port of Vizhinjam and nearby spice-producing hills, from ancient into medieval times.

alchon-huns.name: Alchon Huns
alchon-huns.summary: Nomadic people who ruled parts of Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent in the 4th to 6th centuries CE, whose invasion helped bring down the Gupta Empire.

mihirakula.name: Mihirakula
mihirakula.summary: The second and last Alchon Hun king in northwestern India (515–542), remembered for destroying Buddhist monasteries in his kingdom after turning against Buddhism.

gandhara.name: Gandhara
gandhara.summary: An ancient Indo-Aryan region centered on the Peshawar valley, in what is now northwest Pakistan and northeast Afghanistan, known as an influential Buddhist civilization.

xuanzang.name: Xuanzang
xuanzang.summary: 7th-century Chinese Buddhist monk and traveler (602–664) whose journey to India in 629–645 brought hundreds of Buddhist texts back to China for translation.

aror.name: Aror
aror.summary: Medieval name for the city of Rohri in Sindh, Pakistan, which once served as the capital of Sindh.

mahmud-of-ghazni.name: Mahmud of Ghazni
mahmud-of-ghazni.summary: Sultan of the Ghaznavid Empire from 998 to 1030 whose campaigns extended his rule from Iran to the Punjab, laying the foundation for Muslim rule in the Indian subcontinent.

al-hajjaj-ibn-yusuf.name: Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf
al-hajjaj-ibn-yusuf.summary: A governor (c. 658-714) who served the Umayyad Caliphate, ruling Iraq and the east under two caliphs and instituting reforms such as making Arabic the language of Iraq's tax registers.

jauhar.name: Jauhar
jauhar.summary: A practice of mass self-immolation by Rajput women and children to avoid capture and rape when facing certain defeat in war, most famously at Chittorgarh fort in 1303.

siribhoovalaya.name: Siribhoovalaya
siribhoovalaya.summary: A multi-lingual work by the Jain monk Kumudendu Muni, written entirely in Kannada numerals rather than letters, using patterns across an 18-script, 700-language frame.

kumudendu-muni.name: Kumudendu Muni
kumudendu-muni.summary: Jain monk and polymath from Karnataka, India, around 840 CE, traditionally credited with writing the Siribhoovalaya, a work encoding many subjects entirely in Kannada numeral ciphers.

middle-kingdoms-of-india.name: Middle kingdoms of India
middle-kingdoms-of-india.summary: A term for the political entities on the Indian subcontinent from 230 BCE to 1206 CE, spanning the Classical and early Medieval periods.

adikavi-pampa.name: Pampa
adikavi-pampa.summary: Kannada-language Jain poet (902–955), court poet under king Arikesari II, best known for his epics Vikramarjuna Vijaya and the Adi Purana, models for later Kannada literature.

vikramarjuna-vijaya.name: Vikramarjuna Vijaya
vikramarjuna-vijaya.summary: A 10th-century Kannada epic by the Jain poet Pampa retelling the Mahabharata with Arjuna crowned king instead of Yudhishthira, and credited with founding the Champu poetic style.

lingayats.name: Lingayats
lingayats.summary: A monotheistic Hindu Shaiva sect devoted to Shiva worship via a personal linga symbol, known for rejecting caste and Vedic scripture and for their devotional Vachana poetry.

doha-indian-literature.name: Doha
doha-indian-literature.summary: A two-line rhymed verse form used by Indian poets and bards in North India since about the 6th century CE.

gorakhnath.name: Gorakhnath
gorakhnath.summary: Hindu yogi and saint, around the early 11th century, who founded the Nath monastic movement and is revered as one of nine great masters in its spiritual lineage.

asaga.name: Asaga
asaga.summary: 9th-century Digambara Jain poet who wrote in Sanskrit and Kannada, author in 853 CE of the earliest surviving Sanskrit biography of Mahavira.

mahavira.name: Mahavira
mahavira.summary: Indian religious reformer regarded by Jains as the 24th and final Tirthankara, believed to have lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE; he renounced worldly life around age 30 and preached for 30 years after attaining omniscience.

tirthankara.name: Tirthankara
tirthankara.summary: In Jainism, a supreme teacher who has conquered the cycle of rebirth and shows others the path to liberation; 24 are said to appear in each half-cycle of time, the last being Mahavira.

sivakotiacharya.name: Sivakotiacharya
sivakotiacharya.summary: A Digambara Jain monk, writer and scholar active around the 9th–10th century CE, author of the Vaddaradhane, the earliest known prose work in Kannada.

vaddaradhane.name: Vaddaradhane
vaddaradhane.summary: The earliest known prose work in Kannada, a didactic collection of nineteen stories written by Sivakotiacharya and based on Harisena's Brhatkathakosa.

bhadrab-hu.name: Bhadrabāhu
bhadrab-hu.summary: A Jain monk and scholar (c. 367 to c. 298 BC) traditionally regarded as the last person to possess complete knowledge of the Jain scriptures, and known as the spiritual guru of Chandragupta Maurya.

shravanabelagola.name: Shravanabelagola
shravanabelagola.summary: A town in the Indian state of Karnataka, home to the Gommateshwara Bahubali statue, a major Jain pilgrimage site, where Chandragupta Maurya reportedly died as a Jain monk in 298 BCE.

ranna-kannada-poet.name: Ranna
ranna-kannada-poet.summary: One of the earliest and most celebrated Kannada poets (c. 949–1020), a 'gem' of classical Kannada literature known for martial themes and Jain influence at the Western Chalukya court.

kavirajamarga.name: Kavirajamarga
kavirajamarga.summary: The earliest surviving work on rhetoric, poetics and grammar in the Kannada language, dating to 850 CE and written as a guide for poets.

durvinita.name: Durvinita
durvinita.summary: Ruler of the Western Ganga dynasty from 529 to 579 CE, regarded as its most successful king, noted for military success, literary achievement and patronage of Jainism.

ravikirti.name: Ravikirti
ravikirti.summary: A 7th-century Jain monk, poet and scholar who served as spiritual guru to the Chalukya emperor Pulakeshin II, best known for composing the Aihole inscription celebrating his military achievements.

aihole-inscription.name: Aihole inscription
aihole-inscription.summary: A 7th-century Sanskrit eulogy carved at Aihole's Meguti Jain temple, composed by the poet Ravikirti to honor his patron, Chalukya emperor Pulakeshin II.

shivamara-ii.name: Shivamara II
shivamara-ii.summary: A ruler of the Western Ganga Dynasty in South India from 788 to 816 CE, also a noted scholar in Kannada, Sanskrit and Prakrit.

krishna-iii.name: Pushpadanta
krishna-iii.summary: An Apabhramsha poet patronised by the Rashtrakuta emperor Krishna III (r. 939 to 967), known for writing the Mahapurana and other works.

malkheda.name: Manyakheta (Malkheda)
malkheda.summary: Town in Karnataka, India, formerly called Manyakheta, that served as the imperial capital of the Rashtrakuta dynasty during its 9th to 10th century peak.

uttarapurana.name: Uttarapurana
uttarapurana.summary: A major Jain Sanskrit text forming the second part of the Mahapurana, begun by Acharya Jinasena and completed by his disciple Gunabhadra in the 9th–10th century.

islamic-golden-age.name: Islamic Golden Age
islamic-golden-age.summary: A period of cultural flourishing in Islamic history from the 8th to 14th century, beginning with Baghdad's House of Wisdom under Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid and ending with the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

abbasid-caliphate.name: Abbasid Caliphate
abbasid-caliphate.summary: The third Islamic caliphate, ruling from 750 to 1258 with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time, known for ushering in the Islamic Golden Age of science and culture.

brahmagupta.name: Brahmagupta
brahmagupta.summary: Indian mathematician and astronomer (c. 598–668 CE) credited with formalizing the concept of zero and giving the first clear description of the quadratic formula.

pell-s-equation.name: Pell's equation
pell-s-equation.summary: An equation of the form x²−ny²=1, studied since ancient India, with Brahmagupta finding early solutions and Lagrange later proving it always has infinitely many integer solutions.

hindu-arabic-numeral-system.name: Hindu–Arabic numeral system
hindu-arabic-numeral-system.summary: The base-ten positional number system in common use today, developed by Indian mathematicians between the 1st and 4th centuries and adopted and extended by Arabic mathematicians by the 9th century before spreading to medieval Europe.

al-mansur.name: Al-Mansur
al-mansur.summary: Second Abbasid caliph (714-775) who founded the round city that became the core of Baghdad and is regarded by historians as the true founder of the Abbasid Caliphate.

mu-ammad-ibn-ibr-h-m-al-faz-r.name: Al-Fazari
mu-ammad-ibn-ibr-h-m-al-faz-r.summary: Arab philosopher, mathematician and astronomer who died in 796 or 806.

ya-qub-ibn-tariq.name: Yaqub ibn Tariq
ya-qub-ibn-tariq.summary: Persian astronomer and mathematician who lived in Baghdad and died around 796.

muslim-conquest-of-persia.name: Muslim conquest of Persia
muslim-conquest-of-persia.summary: A military campaign in which the Rashidun Caliphate conquered the Sasanian Empire between 633 and 651 CE, part of the early Muslim conquests that began under Muhammad in 627/628.

dharmakirti.name: Dharmakirti
dharmakirti.summary: An influential 7th-century Indian Buddhist philosopher at Nalanda, a key theorist of Buddhist epistemology and atomism whose work shaped later Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain thought.

dign-ga.name: Dignāga
dign-ga.summary: Indian Buddhist philosopher and logician, c. 470 to 540 CE, credited as a founder of Indian logic and the first system of Buddhist logic and epistemology, influencing later Buddhist and Hindu thinkers.

vaisheshika.name: Vaisheshika
vaisheshika.summary: One of the six classical schools of Hindu philosophy from ancient India, known for developing an atomist theory of the physical universe.

ka-da.name: Kaṇāda
ka-da.summary: Ancient Indian philosopher, active sometime between the 6th and 2nd centuries BCE, who founded the Vaisheshika school and its early theory of atoms.

al-khwarizmi.name: Al-Khwarizmi
al-khwarizmi.summary: A mathematician, astronomer and geographer (c. 780-850) of the Islamic Golden Age who worked at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and is regarded as the father of algebra.

al-kindi.name: Al-Kindi
al-kindi.summary: A Mesopotamian Arab polymath (c. 801-873) hailed as the 'father of Arab philosophy,' who oversaw the translation of Greek texts at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and wrote on subjects from mathematics to medicine.

harun-al-rashid.name: Harun al-Rashid
harun-al-rashid.summary: Fifth Abbasid caliph, reigning 786 to 809, whose rule is traditionally seen as the start of the Islamic Golden Age; he founded the House of Wisdom library in Baghdad.

bhinmal.name: Bhinmal
bhinmal.summary: An ancient town in Rajasthan, India, that served as the early capital of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty and was the birthplace of poet Magha and mathematician-astronomer Brahmagupta.

pala-empire.name: Pala Empire
pala-empire.summary: An early medieval Indian empire based in Bengal and Bihar from the late 8th century, noted for its war elephants and navy and for sponsoring Buddhist institutions.

pratihara-dynasty.name: Pratihara dynasty
pratihara-dynasty.summary: A medieval Indian dynasty ruling from Kannauj between the 8th and 10th centuries, which contained Arab armies advancing from the west and, under Mihira Bhoja, became one of the most powerful states in northern India.

kannauj.name: Kannauj
kannauj.summary: An ancient city in Uttar Pradesh, India, once capital of several kingdoms and long fought over by rival empires for control of the Gangetic Plains.

kanyakumari.name: Kanyakumari
kanyakumari.summary: A town at the southernmost tip of the Indian subcontinent in Tamil Nadu, a pilgrimage and tourist site referenced since the ancient Sangam period.

kalaburagi.name: Kalaburagi
kalaburagi.summary: A city in the Indian state of Karnataka, formerly known as Gulbarga, home to notable religious structures and monuments built under Bahmani rule.

mahendravarman-i.name: Mahendravarman I
mahendravarman-i.summary: Pallava emperor who ruled parts of southern India from 590 to 630, and was also a scholar, painter, architect and musician.

narasimhavarman-i.name: Narasimhavarman I
narasimhavarman-i.summary: A Pallava emperor who reigned from 630 to 668, completing monuments at Mamallapuram begun by his father and avenging an earlier defeat by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II.

chola-dynasty.name: Chola dynasty
chola-dynasty.summary: A Tamil dynasty from southern India that built an expansive maritime empire, reaching its height in the 9th to 13th centuries CE under rulers such as Rajaraja I.

aditya-i.name: Aditya I
aditya-i.summary: Chola king who reigned in the late ninth to early tenth century, son of Vijayalaya Chola, who founded the Medieval Cholas by conquering the Pallava kingdom and occupying the Western Ganga kingdom and Kongu Nadu.

dantidurga.name: Dantidurga
dantidurga.summary: Ruler from 753 to 756 CE who founded the Rashtrakuta Empire based in Karnataka, defeating the Chalukyas and other regional kings.

kirtivarman-ii.name: Kirtivarman II
kirtivarman-ii.summary: The last ruler of the Badami Chalukya dynasty, reigning from 746 to 753, whose rule was undermined by the rising power of the Rashtrakutas and Pandyas.

nagabhata-i.name: Nagabhata I
nagabhata-i.summary: Founder of the imperial Pratihara dynasty in northern India, ruling roughly 730 to 760 CE from Ujjain, who repelled an Arab invasion from Sindh.

nagabhata-ii.name: Nagabhata II
nagabhata-ii.summary: Emperor of the Pratihara dynasty from 795 to 833 who took grand imperial titles after conquering the city of Kannauj.

mihira-bhoja.name: Mihira Bhoja
mihira-bhoja.summary: A Pratihara emperor of northern India (r. c. 836–885) who turned a weakened realm into a large, prosperous empire reaching from the Narmada to the Sutlej.

mahendrapala-i.name: Mahendrapala I
mahendrapala-i.summary: Emperor of Aryavarta and King of Kannauj from 885 to 910, a member of the Pratihara dynasty who ruled a vast northern Indian empire and appears under several other recorded names.

indra-iii.name: Indra III
indra-iii.summary: Rashtrakuta emperor who ruled from 914 until his death in 929, grandson of Krishna II, remembered for patronizing Kannada and Sanskrit poets.

paramara-dynasty.name: Paramara dynasty
paramara-dynasty.summary: A dynasty ruling the Malwa region of west-central India from 948 to 1305, reaching its greatest extent under king Bhoja before being defeated by Delhi's forces in 1305.

chandelas-of-jejakabhukti.name: Chandelas of Jejakabhukti
chandelas-of-jejakabhukti.summary: An Indian dynasty that ruled the Bundelkhand region of central India from the 9th to 13th centuries, remembered for building the temples of Khajuraho.

gwalior-fort.name: Gwalior Fort
gwalior-fort.summary: A hill fort in Gwalior dating to at least the 6th century, called the 'pearl amongst the fortresses of Hind' by Mughal emperor Babur and nicknamed the 'Gibraltar of India'.

kalabhra-dynasty.name: Kalabhra dynasty
kalabhra-dynasty.summary: A dynasty that ruled parts of the Tamil region between the 3rd and 6th centuries CE, displacing the earlier Chola, Pandya and Chera dynasties in what is called the 'dark period' of Tamil history.

vijayalaya-chola.name: Vijayalaya Chola
vijayalaya-chola.summary: Ruler from 850 to 871 who founded the Imperial Chola Dynasty, re-establishing Chola power over the region north of the Kaveri river.

rajendra-i.name: Rajendra I
rajendra-i.summary: Chola emperor who reigned from 1014 to 1044, under whom the empire reached its peak, extending rule across the Indian Ocean into Southeast Asia.

srivijaya.name: Srivijaya
srivijaya.summary: A Buddhist thalassocratic empire based on Sumatra from the 7th to 11th century that dominated much of maritime Southeast Asia and its trade routes, especially with China.

al-masudi.name: Al-Masudi
al-masudi.summary: A historian, geographer and traveler (c. 896–956), sometimes called the 'Herodotus of the Arabs,' best known for his magnum opus The Meadows of Gold, blending history, geography and biography.

konkan.name: Konkan
konkan.summary: A coastal strip of western India between the Arabian Sea and the Deccan Plateau, known by name since Strabo's time and home to a thriving Arab trading port from the 10th century.

nalanda-mahavihara.name: Nalanda
nalanda-mahavihara.summary: A renowned Buddhist monastery and centre of learning in medieval Bihar, India, operating from about 427 to 1400 CE and often called the world's first residential university.

adi-shankara.name: Adi Shankara
adi-shankara.summary: 8th-century Indian Vedic scholar-monk and philosopher of Advaita Vedanta, later revered as a major religious leader, though little reliable information survives about his actual life.

advaita-vedanta.name: Advaita Vedanta
advaita-vedanta.summary: Hindu philosophical tradition holding that the individual self is ultimately identical with the universal Brahman, and that liberation comes from realizing this oneness.

trika.name: Pratyabhijña
trika.summary: A nondual philosophy of "recognition" within Kashmir Shaiva tantra, teaching that one must recognize oneself as divine, developed by Utpaladeva (c. 925-975) and Abhinavagupta (c. 975-1025).

utpaladeva.name: Utpaladeva
utpaladeva.summary: A 10th-century Kashmiri Shaiva philosopher and poet of the Pratyabhijñā school, whose ideas were later developed by the more famous Abhinavagupta.

abhinavagupta.name: Abhinavagupta
abhinavagupta.summary: Philosopher, mystic and aesthetician from Kashmir (c. 950–1016 CE) who wrote over 35 works, including an encyclopedic treatise on Kashmir Shaivism, and shaped Indian aesthetics.

tantra.name: Tantra
tantra.summary: An esoteric yogic tradition developed in the Indian subcontinent from the mid-1st millennium CE, using mantras and rituals within Hinduism and Buddhism.

gupta-empire.name: Gupta Empire
gupta-empire.summary: An Indian empire from the mid-3rd to mid-6th century CE that ruled much of northern India, a period often called India's Golden Age for its cultural and scientific advances.

agama-hinduism.name: Agamas
agama-hinduism.summary: A body of Tantric Hindu scriptures in Sanskrit and Tamil covering cosmology, meditation, and temple worship, in existence by around the mid-1st millennium CE.

chaturanga.name: Chaturanga
chaturanga.summary: An ancient Indian strategy board game known from around the 7th century CE, considered the common ancestor of chess and related games across Asia.

dambal.name: Dambal
dambal.summary: A village in Karnataka, India, that was an ancient center of Buddhism, remaining so as late as the 12th century.

balligavi.name: Balligavi
balligavi.summary: A town in Karnataka, India, known for ancient monuments and once an important Jain center with more than twenty basadis recorded before the 12th century.

kayalpatnam.name: Kayalpatnam
kayalpatnam.summary: A historic coastal town in Tamil Nadu, India, long known for its centuries-old maritime trade and Islamic heritage.

nagore.name: Nagore
nagore.summary: A town in Tamil Nadu, India, known for the Nagore Dargah, a 16th-century Islamic shrine drawing millions of pilgrims of every faith.
